passage:
I share a flat with Mohit, so I noticed the phone calls. Mohit's college friend had started giving nearly all savings and every weekend to a group. Mohit never lectured. Every Thursday Mohit rang: "How was your week? What's the best part? How do you decide how much to give?"

Once the friend hung up sharply. Mohit just sent a silly picture and, "Still on for dosa on Saturday?"

I'm Sudha, and I told Mohit to say plainly that it was a trap. Mohit shook a head. "If I attack the group, I lose my friend. Then who do they call when doubts come?"

Last week the friend rang at midnight, voice shaky. "Can I ask you something?"

I can't tell how worried Mohit is inside. I only saw Mohit's face when the phone lit up.

qa.q: How often did Mohit ring the friend?
Why did Mohit choose not to attack the group?
qa.a: Mohit feared losing the friend: if the group were attacked, the friend might not call Mohit when doubts arrived.
More open questions about what the group asks for and how the friend decides how much to give, while staying warm and keeping plans like the dosa on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Sudha see Mohit's approach?
qa.a: Sudha first wanted Mohit to say plainly that it was a trap, but the midnight call from the friend shows why staying in touch mattered.

grounding: Mohit worries about a friend giving all savings and time to a group, stays warm, asks open questions and keeps the friendship alive.

passage:
Gabriel noticed Sofia's apartment in Madrid was nearly empty. The couch, the bookshelf, even the old piano were gone.

"I sold them," she said happily. "The community is building a retreat house. Everything I give helps."

Gabriel felt his chest tighten. He wanted to say, They're using you. He could picture her face closing if he did.

"You look happy," he said instead, and meant it. "What do you love most about them?"

She talked for twenty minutes about the morning silence, the songs, the woman who had held her when her father died.

"Is there anything that ever bothers you there?" he asked.

Sofia hesitated. "Sometimes they get upset when I see old friends."

"Well, this old friend is taking you for churros on Sunday," Gabriel said. "Same as always."

She laughed. On the way out, he told himself: stay close. Keep the door open.

qa.a: Her couch, her bookshelf and her old piano.

qa.q: What was Gabriel feeling when he saw the empty apartment?
qa.a: He felt worried and tense, his chest tightening at how much Sofia was giving away.

qa.q: Why was asking open questions wiser than saying "They're using you"?
qa.a: Open questions let Sofia talk without defending herself, and one even led her to admit something that bothers her, while an attack would have closed her off.

qa.q: How does Sofia see Gabriel's visit?
qa.a: Sofia seems glad and relaxed with him, happy to share what she loves and pleased to keep their Sunday churros.

grounding: The passage shows a friend worried that someone is giving everything to a group, staying warm, asking open questions and keeping the friendship alive rather than attacking her belief.

passage:
In the Gurugram office, Akash had once been the one who stayed late to help everyone. Now he left at five sharp for his spiritual group, and at lunch he talked about giving the group his whole bonus.

Swati watched him skip a third team dinner. She was worried. She also knew Akash well enough to know that mocking the group would end their friendship.

She caught him at the coffee machine. "Hey. I miss you at dinners. How's your group going?"

He brightened. "They're like family."

"That's lovely. What's a normal week like there?"

He described it. Long evenings. Weekends. "They say doubts mean my ego is fighting."

"And do you have doubts?"

He looked at his cup. "Sometimes."

"You can always tell me about them," Swati said. "No judgement. And come to Friday's dinner. We'll save you a seat."

He came. He stayed an hour.

qa.q: What did Akash say the group tells him about doubts?
qa.a: "They say doubts mean my ego is fighting."

qa.q: What was Swati worried about when Akash skipped a third team dinner?
qa.a: She was anxious that Akash was giving the group all his time and money, and afraid that mocking it would end their friendship.

qa.q: What could Swati keep doing to help Akash?
qa.a: Stay warm, keep asking open questions, and keep inviting him to things, so he has someone to turn to when doubts grow.

qa.q: How might Akash see Swati's question at the coffee machine?
qa.a: Akash seems glad to be asked kindly and safe enough to admit he sometimes has doubts.

grounding: The passage shows a colleague worried about a friend giving his time and money to a group, staying warm, asking open questions and keeping the friendship alive without attacking his belief.
